title: Imports and Namespaces
content: Imports the full Mathlib library and opens `Set`, `Cardinal`, `Ordinal` namespaces. This gives access to cardinal arithmetic ($2^{\aleph_0}$), ordinal operations ($\omega + n$, $\omega^2$), and the `Finset` API.
mathContext: The formalization uses `Cardinal.continuum`, `Ordinal.omega0`, `Cardinal.aleph0`, and `Ordinal.card` from Mathlib to connect ordinals, cardinals, and set-theoretic partition relations.

title: Coloring of n-Element Subsets
content: Defines **Coloring S n k** as a function from $n$-element subsets of $S$ (as subtypes) to $\text{Fin}(k)$ colors. This is the basic object of partition calculus.
mathContext: A $k$-coloring of $[S]^n$ is a function $c: \binom{S}{n} \to k$. The partition arrow $\kappa \to (\alpha, \beta)_k^n$ asks what monochromatic subsets are guaranteed to exist for any such coloring.

title: n-Element Subsets
content: Defines **nSubsets S n** as the set of all Finsets of S with cardinality exactly n. This is $[S]^n = \{t \subseteq S \mid |t| = n\}$.
mathContext: The set $[S]^n$ of $n$-element subsets is the domain of colorings in partition calculus. For the problem, $n = 3$ (3-element subsets).

title: Homogeneous Set
content: Defines **IsHomogeneous H n c i**: all $n$-subsets of $H$ receive color $i$ under coloring $c$. This is the Ramsey-theoretic notion of a monochromatic set.
mathContext: A set $H \subseteq S$ is $i$-homogeneous for coloring $c: [S]^n \to k$ if $c(t) = i$ for all $t \in [H]^n$. The partition arrow guarantees either a large color-0 homogeneous set or a finite color-1 homogeneous set.

title: Finset Homogeneous Set
content: Defines **FinsetIsHomogeneous H n k c i**: the Finset variant of homogeneity. All $n$-subsets of the finite set $H$ receive color $i$. Used for the finite parameter in the partition arrow.
mathContext: The finite homogeneous set is needed for the second alternative in $\kappa \to (\alpha, m)_2^3$: a finite monochromatic set of size $\ge m$ for color 1.

title: Order Type Bound
content: Defines **HasOrderTypeAtLeast S H α**: the cardinality of $H$ is at least $|\alpha|$. A simplified approximation of the full order-type condition $\text{otp}(H, <) \ge \alpha$.
mathContext: The full definition would require $H$ to carry a well-ordering of order type $\ge \alpha$. The cardinal approximation $|H| \ge |\alpha|$ is necessary but not sufficient; however, for countable ordinals and uncountable sets, the distinction is often immaterial.

title: Partition Arrow κ → (α, m)₂³
content: Defines **PartitionArrow κ α m**: for any 2-coloring of 3-element subsets of a set of cardinality κ, either there exists a color-0 homogeneous set of order type ≥ α, or a color-1 homogeneous Finset of size ≥ m.
mathContext: The arrow notation $\kappa \to (\alpha, m)_2^3$ is the central concept of partition calculus. The asymmetry between $\alpha$ (an ordinal, for color 0) and $m$ (a natural number, for color 1) reflects the typical setup where one seeks a large structured set or a small finite one.

title: Continuum Cardinal 𝔠 = 2^ℵ₀
content: Defines **continuum_card** = Cardinal.continuum = $2^{\aleph_0}$, the cardinality of the real numbers. Proves the defining equation `continuum_def : continuum_card = 2 ^ aleph0`.
mathContext: The continuum $\mathfrak{c} = 2^{\aleph_0}$ is the cardinality of $\mathbb{R}$, $\mathcal{P}(\mathbb{N})$, and $\{0,1\}^{\mathbb{N}}$. Under GCH, $\mathfrak{c} = \aleph_1$; in general, $\mathfrak{c} \ge \aleph_1$ but could be much larger.

title: Countable Ordinal
content: Defines **IsCountableOrdinal α**: an ordinal α has cardinality $|\alpha| \le \aleph_0$. All ordinals $< \omega_1$ are countable. The problem quantifies over all such ordinals.
mathContext: The countable ordinals form the set $\omega_1 = \{\alpha \mid |\alpha| \le \aleph_0\}$, the first uncountable ordinal. Examples: $\omega$, $\omega + n$, $\omega^2$, $\omega^\omega$, $\varepsilon_0$. Problem #70 asks about partition properties for ALL of these.

title: ω is Countable
content: Proves **omega0_countable**: $|\omega| = \aleph_0 \le \aleph_0$, so $\omega$ is a countable ordinal. Uses `card_omega0` from Mathlib.
mathContext: The first infinite ordinal $\omega = \{0, 1, 2, \ldots\}$ has cardinality $|\omega| = \aleph_0$. This is the base case for the hierarchy of countable ordinals.

title: Erdős-Rado: 𝔠 → (ω+n, 4)₂³
content: **Erdős-Rado Theorem**: For all $2 \le n < \omega$, $\mathfrak{c} \to (\omega + n, 4)_2^3$. This is the strongest known partial result toward the full conjecture, proved using the stepping-up lemma.
mathContext: The stepping-up lemma converts $\kappa \to (\alpha, m)_2^2$ to $\kappa \to (\alpha', m+1)_2^3$ for a related ordinal $\alpha'$. Starting from $\mathfrak{c} \to (\omega, 3)_2^2$ (which follows from the infinite Ramsey theorem), stepping up gives $\mathfrak{c} \to (\omega + n, 4)_2^3$.

title: Erdős Problem 70 (OPEN)
content: **Main Conjecture**: For all countable ordinals $\beta$ and $n \ge 2$, $\mathfrak{c} \to (\beta, n)_2^3$. The general case beyond $\omega + n$ remains completely OPEN.
mathContext: The conjecture asserts $\forall \beta < \omega_1, \forall n \ge 2: \mathfrak{c} \to (\beta, n)_2^3$. The first genuinely open case is $\beta = \omega \cdot 2$ (or equivalently $\omega^2$), since $\omega + n$ is covered by Erdős-Rado.

title: Special Case: β = ω
content: Defines **conjecture_omega(n)**: $\mathfrak{c} \to (\omega, n)_2^3$. This follows from the Erdős-Rado theorem by monotonicity ($\omega \le \omega + n$).
mathContext: Since $\omega \le \omega + n$ for $n \ge 0$, and $\mathfrak{c} \to (\omega+n, 4)_2^3$ by Erdős-Rado, monotonicity gives $\mathfrak{c} \to (\omega, 4)_2^3$, and then $\mathfrak{c} \to (\omega, n)_2^3$ for $n \le 4$.

title: Special Case: β = ω²
content: Defines **conjecture_omega_squared(n)**: $\mathfrak{c} \to (\omega^2, n)_2^3$. This is the first genuinely open case, strictly beyond the Erdős-Rado result.
mathContext: The ordinal $\omega^2 = \omega \cdot \omega$ has order type 'ω copies of ω'. Since $\omega^2 > \omega + n$ for all finite $n$, the Erdős-Rado theorem does not cover this case. Whether $\mathfrak{c} \to (\omega^2, n)_2^3$ holds is unknown.

title: Special Case: β = ω^ω
content: Defines **conjecture_omega_tower(n)**: $\mathfrak{c} \to (\omega^\omega, n)_2^3$. The ordinal $\omega^\omega = \sup(\omega, \omega^2, \omega^3, \ldots)$ is a limit ordinal strictly larger than any $\omega^k$.
mathContext: The ordinal $\omega^\omega$ is the first ordinal that cannot be expressed as $\omega^k$ for finite $k$. It is countable ($|\omega^\omega| = \aleph_0$) and well below $\varepsilon_0$. This would be a significantly stronger result than $\omega^2$.

title: Finite Ramsey Theorem
content: **Finite Ramsey Theorem**: For any $r, k, n$, there exists $N$ such that any $k$-coloring of $n$-subsets of an $N$-set has a monochromatic $r$-set. This is the finite analogue of partition calculus.
mathContext: The finite Ramsey theorem $N \to (r)_k^n$ (where $N = R_k^n(r, \ldots, r)$) is the starting point for all of Ramsey theory. The infinite partition calculus generalizes this to infinite cardinals and ordinals.

title: R(3,3) = 6
content: **Ramsey's Theorem (specific)**: Any 2-coloring of 3-subsets of a 6-element set has a monochromatic 3-subset. This is the classical $R(3,3) = 6$ result.
mathContext: The Ramsey number $R(3,3) = 6$ is one of the few exactly known values. It means that among any 6 people, there are either 3 mutual friends or 3 mutual strangers (in the edge-coloring version). The hypergraph version stated here is for 3-uniform hypergraphs.

title: Counterexample Structure
content: Defines **erdos_70_counterexample**: the negation of the conjecture — there exist a countable $\beta$ and $n \ge 2$ with $\mathfrak{c} \not\to (\beta, n)_2^3$. This would give a coloring with no large monochromatic subsets.
mathContext: A counterexample would provide a specific 2-coloring $c$ of $[\mathfrak{c}]^3$ such that no color-0 homogeneous set has order type $\ge \beta$ and no color-1 homogeneous set has size $\ge n$.

title: Conjecture ↔ ¬Counterexample
content: Proves the conjecture and counterexample are logically complementary: `erdos_70_conjecture ↔ ¬erdos_70_counterexample`. The proof is by unfolding definitions and applying `push_neg`.
mathContext: This is a logical tautology: $\forall \beta, n, P(\beta, n)$ is equivalent to $\neg \exists \beta, n, \neg P(\beta, n)$. The `push_neg` tactic handles the negation pushing automatically.

title: Ordinal Monotonicity of Partition Arrows
content: If $\kappa \to (\beta, m)_2^3$ and $\alpha \le \beta$, then $\kappa \to (\alpha, m)_2^3$. Smaller ordinals are easier to find as homogeneous sets — any color-0 set of type $\ge \beta$ also has type $\ge \alpha$.
mathContext: Monotonicity in the first ordinal parameter follows from transitivity of $\le$: if $|H| \ge |\beta| \ge |\alpha|$ then $|H| \ge |\alpha|$. This is why the Erdős-Rado result for $\omega + n$ implies the result for $\omega$.

title: Size Monotonicity of Partition Arrows
content: If $\kappa \to (\alpha, n)_2^3$ and $m \le n$, then $\kappa \to (\alpha, m)_2^3$. Smaller finite sets are easier to find — any color-1 homogeneous set of size $\ge n$ also has size $\ge m$.
mathContext: Monotonicity in the finite parameter follows from $|H| \ge n \ge m$. Combined with ordinal monotonicity, this means the partition arrow becomes 'harder' as both parameters increase.

title: ω + n is Countable
content: Proves $\omega + n$ is a countable ordinal: $|\omega + n| = \aleph_0 + n = \aleph_0$ by cardinal absorption. Uses `card_add`, `card_omega0`, `card_nat`, and `aleph0_add_nat`.
mathContext: Cardinal arithmetic gives $\aleph_0 + n = \aleph_0$ for finite $n$ (infinite cardinal absorption). This shows $\omega + n$ falls within the scope of the conjecture for all $n < \omega$.

title: ω² is Countable
content: Proves $\omega^2 = \omega \cdot \omega$ is countable: $|\omega^2| = \aleph_0 \cdot \aleph_0 = \aleph_0$. Uses `card_mul`, `card_omega0`, and `aleph0_mul_aleph0`.
mathContext: The ordinal $\omega^2$ has the same cardinality as $\omega$ ($\aleph_0 \cdot \aleph_0 = \aleph_0$), but a richer order structure. This is why $\omega^2$ represents a genuinely harder case for partition relations despite having the same cardinality.
